Effect of a hypothetical intervention on binary exposures

intervene_effect.Rd

Estimates \(\psi = E[Y^{g_1}] - E[Y^{g_0}]\), the population effect on an outcome of intervening on some binary exposures (for example selected indicators of a childhood adversity latent class model), adjusting for the other exposures and the confounders, with the parametric g-formula, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), augmented IPW (AIPW) or targeted maximum likelihood (TMLE). Interventions are static (setto()), stochastic (shift()) or the natural course (natural()). The intervention is defined on observed exposures, never by assigning people to latent classes.

Usage

intervene_effect(
  data,
  outcome,
  exposures,
  intervene,
  confounders = NULL,
  g1,
  g0 = natural(),
  estimator = "aipw",
  family = c("gaussian", "binomial"),
  outcome_model = "linear",
  propensity_model = "linear",
  folds = 5,
  B = 200,
  seed = 1,
  adjust = c("exposures", "classes", "both"),
  adjust_K = NULL,
  adjust_model = NULL,
  learners = NULL,
  bound = 0.01
)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

outcome

The outcome column (tidyselect; one column). Numeric; logical or two-level factor outcomes are coded 0/1.

exposures

The binary exposure columns (tidyselect, e.g. ace1:ace8; 0/1, logical or two-level factors).

intervene

The exposures that are intervened on, selected among exposures (tidyselect; 1 to 6 columns). Their order is the order of the setto() values.

confounders

Confounder columns (tidyselect; factors are dummy-coded), or NULL. Columns that are the outcome or exposures are dropped with a warning.

g1, g0

Interventions compared (setto(), shift(), natural()); g0 defaults to the natural course.

estimator

"aipw" (default), "tmle", "gformula" or "ipw".

family

"gaussian" (continuous outcome; \(\psi\) is a mean difference) or "binomial" (0/1 outcome; \(\psi\) is a risk difference).

outcome_model, propensity_model

Working models: "linear" or "quadratic" (see Details).

folds

Number of cross-fitting folds (1 = no cross-fitting).

B

Bootstrap replications for the g-formula standard error.

seed

Random seed (folds and bootstrap).

adjust

What the adjustment set \(H\) contains: "exposures" (default; the non-intervened exposures and the confounders), "classes" (the posterior probabilities of classes \(1, \dots, K-1\) of a latent class model of the non-intervened exposures only with the confounders as covariates, plus the confounders) or "both". See intervene_within() and the package documentation page Latent classes and interventions.

adjust_K, adjust_model

Number of classes of that model (fitted in Julia), or a fitted latentmixtures::lca() model of the non-intervened exposures (same rows).

learners

Machine-learning nuisance models. Besides "linear" and "quadratic", outcome_model and propensity_model accept a learner fitted within the cross-fitting training folds: "lasso", "lasso_quadratic", "elasticnet", "ridge", "forest", "boost" (needs EvoTrees.jl) or "superlearner". A learner for the outcome is fitted within each exposure pattern (or, with rare patterns, to the intervened exposures and \(H\) with the exposures unpenalised) and evaluated at every exposure pattern; a learner for the propensity is fitted to each link of the chain. learners is the library of the "superlearner": learner names ("mean", "glm", "glm_quadratic", "lasso", "lasso_quadratic", "elasticnet", "ridge", "forest", "boost"), or NULL for the default library (mean, glm, lasso, lasso_quadratic, forest).

bound

With a propensity learner, every conditional probability of the chain is bounded to [bound, 1 - bound]. Not applied to "linear" / "quadratic".

Value

An object of class intervention_result, a list with

psi1, psi0, effect

\(E[Y^{g_1}]\), \(E[Y^{g_0}]\) and \(\psi\);

se_psi1, se_psi0, se

their standard errors;

estimator, family, outcome_model, propensity_model, folds

the settings;

n, n_dropped

rows used and rows dropped for missing values;

min_pi, max_weight

positivity diagnostics;

g1, g0, g1_label, g0_label

descriptions of the interventions;

outcome, exposures, intervene, confounders, call

variable names and the call;

propensity

the cross-fitted propensities, per analysed row: pattern (observed pattern of the intervened exposures, e.g. "01"), w1, w0 (weights of g1 and g0) and pi (matrix of \(\pi(s \mid H)\), one column per pattern), with relevant flagging the patterns that receive probability under g1 or g0; used by autoplot() (type = "overlap", "weights");

text

Julia's printed summary.

Methods: print(), tidy(), glance(), as.data.frame(), coef(), nobs(), causal_table(), lm_table(), autoplot() and causal_plot().

Details

Identification. Let \(S\) be the intervened exposures and \(H\) the other exposures and the confounders. \(E[Y^g] = E[\sum_s q(s \mid A_S, H)\mu(s, H)]\) with \(\mu(s, H) = E[Y \mid A_S = s, H]\) and \(q\) the intervention distribution, under (1) consistency; (2) conditional exchangeability, \(Y^s \perp A_S \mid H\); (3) positivity of the exposure profiles that the intervention puts mass on; and (4) the other exposures in \(H\) are not affected by \(A_S\) (otherwise they are mediators and adjusting for them changes the estimand). If a latent variable that generates the exposures (e.g. a family context underlying adversity classes) also affects the outcome directly, adjusting for the other exposures is only proxy adjustment, (2) fails and \(\psi\) is biased whatever the estimator.

Estimators.

  • "gformula": parametric g-formula (Robins 1986), with the outcome model cross-fitted over folds like the other estimators. Standard errors come from a nonparametric bootstrap (B replications) that applies the same estimator to each resample (outcome model cross-fitted over the same folds), so the SE belongs to the reported estimate; folds = 1 gives the plain plug-in g-formula.

  • "ipw": Hájek-normalised IPTW with weight \(g^*(A_S \mid H)/\pi(A_S \mid H)\); influence-function standard errors. IPTW for stochastic interventions: Muñoz & van der Laan (2012).

  • "aipw": augmented IPW (Bang & Robins 2005; for stochastic interventions, Muñoz & van der Laan 2012 and Díaz et al. 2023); doubly robust.

  • "tmle": targeted maximum likelihood (van der Laan & Rose 2011; for stochastic interventions, Muñoz & van der Laan 2012); doubly robust and respects the bounds of a binary outcome.

The propensity \(\pi\) is a chain of logistic regressions \(P(A_j \mid A_{S,<j}, H)\); the outcome model \(\mu\) is linear ("gaussian") or logistic ("binomial") in \((A_S, H)\) for "linear", or saturated in \(A_S\) with squares, products and \(A_S \times H\) interactions for "quadratic". Both are cross-fitted over folds. The minimum post-intervention profile probability (min_pi) and the largest weight (max_weight) diagnose positivity; the print method warns when min_pi < 0.01.

Missing data. Rows with a missing value in the outcome, exposures or confounders are dropped (with a message); the number used is in $n and the number dropped in $n_dropped.

How to use

  1. Select the binary exposures (exposures = ace1:ace8) and, among them, the ones to intervene on (intervene, 1 to 6 columns); the other exposures and the confounders are adjusted for.

  2. Choose g1 (setto(), shift(), subgroup() or intervention()) and g0 (default natural(), the observed course). setto() values follow the order of intervene.

  3. Set family = "binomial" for a 0/1 outcome (\(\psi\) is then a risk difference); keep estimator = "aipw" or use "tmle".

  4. Check overlap (min_pi, max_weight; autoplot(r, type = "weights")); with rare exposure profiles, compare adjust = "classes" and adjust = "both".

  5. Vary the nuisance models (outcome_model = "quadratic", learners) and probe latent confounding by the exposure classes with intervene_latent_sensitivity(). See vignette("function-guide").

References

Bang, H., & Robins, J. M. (2005). Doubly robust estimation in missing data and causal inference models. Biometrics, 61(4), 962–973. doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00377.x

Díaz, I., Williams, N., Hoffman, K. L., & Schenck, E. J. (2023). Nonparametric causal effects based on longitudinal modified treatment policies. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 118(542), 846–857. doi:10.1080/01621459.2021.1955691

Haneuse, S., & Rotnitzky, A. (2013). Estimation of the effect of interventions that modify the received treatment. Statistics in Medicine, 32(30), 5260–5277. doi:10.1002/sim.5907

Hernán, M. A., & Robins, J. M. (2020). Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Muñoz, I. D., & van der Laan, M. (2012). Population intervention causal effects based on stochastic interventions. Biometrics, 68(2), 541–549. doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01685.x

Robins, J. (1986). A new approach to causal inference in mortality studies with a sustained exposure period: Application to control of the healthy worker survivor effect. Mathematical Modelling, 7(9–12), 1393–1512. doi:10.1016/0270-0255(86)90088-6

van der Laan, M. J., & Rose, S. (2011). Targeted Learning: Causal Inference for Observational and Experimental Data. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4419-9782-1

See also

intervention_effect_matrix() for vectors and matrices; natural(); intervene_membership(); tidy.intervention_result(), causal_table().

Examples

data(ace_study)
# \donttest{
# Question: would preventing childhood abuse and neglect (ace1, ace2) lower the risk of
# past-year depression? The other six ACEs, age, sex and parental education are adjusted for.
rd <- intervene_effect(ace_study, outcome = depressed, exposures = ace1:ace8,
                       intervene = c(ace1, ace2), confounders = c(age, female, parent_edu),
                       g1 = setto(c(0, 0)), family = "binomial")
#> Starting Julia ...
rd
#> ▸ Effect of a hypothetical intervention on exposures
#>   AIPW, 5-fold cross-fitting, binomial outcome; N = 2500
#>   Outcome:      depressed
#>   Intervene:    ace1, ace2
#>   Adjusted for: ace3, ace4, ace5, ace6, ace7, ace8, age, female, parent_edu
#>   g1:           set to (0, 0)
#>   g0:           natural course
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>                        Estimate     SE            95% CI      p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   E[Yᵍ¹]                  0.129  0.009    [0.112, 0.147]       
#>   E[Yᵍ⁰]                  0.163  0.007    [0.149, 0.178]       
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ψ = E[Yᵍ¹] − E[Yᵍ⁰]    −0.034  0.007  [−0.047, −0.021]  <.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#>   Overlap: min P(A_S = s | H) = 0.0050, max weight = 10.1
#>   ⚠ near-violation of positivity: some post-intervention profiles are rare
# E[Y^g1] = 0.129 (risk if both were prevented), E[Y^g0] = 0.163 (observed course):
# psi = -0.034, a risk difference of 3.4 points (95\% CI -0.047 to -0.021; true -0.038).
# min P(A_S = s | H) = 0.005 < 0.01, so the print method warns that some
# post-intervention profiles are rare; max weight 10.1.

# Halving their prevalence instead (each present exposure removed with probability 0.5)
ace_study |>
  intervene_effect(outcome = depressed, exposures = ace1:ace8,
                   intervene = c(ace1, ace2), confounders = c(age, female, parent_edu),
                   g1 = shift(0.5), family = "binomial")
#> ▸ Effect of a hypothetical intervention on exposures
#>   AIPW, 5-fold cross-fitting, binomial outcome; N = 2500
#>   Outcome:      depressed
#>   Intervene:    ace1, ace2
#>   Adjusted for: ace3, ace4, ace5, ace6, ace7, ace8, age, female, parent_edu
#>   g1:           shift 1→0 with probability 0.5
#>   g0:           natural course
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>                        Estimate     SE            95% CI      p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   E[Yᵍ¹]                  0.143  0.007    [0.128, 0.157]       
#>   E[Yᵍ⁰]                  0.163  0.007    [0.149, 0.178]       
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ψ = E[Yᵍ¹] − E[Yᵍ⁰]    −0.020  0.003  [−0.026, −0.015]  <.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#>   Overlap: min P(A_S = s | H) = 0.0050, max weight = 4.0
#>   ⚠ near-violation of positivity: some post-intervention profiles are rare
# psi = -0.020 (true -0.021): about 60\% of the effect of full prevention

# Continuous outcome: self-rated health (0-100) would be 2.26 points higher
# (95\% CI 1.86 to 2.67; true +2.00)
ace_study |>
  intervene_effect(outcome = health, exposures = ace1:ace8, intervene = c(ace1, ace2),
                   confounders = c(age, female, parent_edu), g1 = setto(c(0, 0)))
#> ▸ Effect of a hypothetical intervention on exposures
#>   AIPW, 5-fold cross-fitting, gaussian outcome; N = 2500
#>   Outcome:      health
#>   Intervene:    ace1, ace2
#>   Adjusted for: ace3, ace4, ace5, ace6, ace7, ace8, age, female, parent_edu
#>   g1:           set to (0, 0)
#>   g0:           natural course
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>                        Estimate     SE            95% CI      p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   E[Yᵍ¹]                 78.965  0.305  [78.367, 79.563]       
#>   E[Yᵍ⁰]                 76.701  0.255  [76.202, 77.201]       
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ψ = E[Yᵍ¹] − E[Yᵍ⁰]     2.264  0.208    [1.855, 2.673]  <.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#>   Overlap: min P(A_S = s | H) = 0.0050, max weight = 10.1
#>   ⚠ near-violation of positivity: some post-intervention profiles are rare

# Robustness to rare profiles: summarise the other six ACEs by their latent class
mr <- latentmixtures::lca(ace_study, ace3:ace8, K = 3, covariates = c(age, female, parent_edu))
rc <- intervene_effect(ace_study, outcome = depressed, exposures = ace1:ace8,
                       intervene = c(ace1, ace2), confounders = c(age, female, parent_edu),
                       g1 = setto(c(0, 0)), family = "binomial",
                       adjust = "classes", adjust_model = mr)
c(effect = rc$effect, max_weight = rc$max_weight)  # -0.035 with max weight 3.0 (vs 10.1)
#>      effect  max_weight 
#> -0.03521508  2.97518639 
# }
